theory.text: IELTS SPEAKING
Part 2
A step-by-step self-study guide
Understand cue cards • Plan in one minute • Develop a two-minute talk • Practise full long turns

rows: Understand the task, cue-card prompts, planning, organisation, language and delivery.
Practise selecting ideas, making keyword notes, sequencing events and extending ideas.
Exercises E1–E10; suggested answers at the end.
Create quick keyword plans without writing complete scripts.
Prepare for one minute, then speak for up to two minutes and record your attempt.
Compare your plan and delivery with suggested answers and model talks.
All keys and model responses at the end.

theory.text: A study routine you can repeat

Session 1: Read one theory section and speak the worked examples aloud. Session 2: complete two or three small exercises. Session 3: plan two cue cards using keywords only. Session 4: record one full long turn, review it and repeat the weakest section.

Practise the IELTS Speaking Part 2 pattern: one minute to prepare, followed by a long turn of one to two minutes. These are task conditions, not a requirement to speak at exactly the same speed or use every second.
Important: model talks are examples, not scripts to memorise. Replace people, places, events and opinions with details that match your own experience.
Part 1 – Theory
1. Understand the task

In IELTS Speaking Part 2, the examiner gives you a task card (often called a cue card). It asks you to talk about a person, place, object, experience, activity or idea. You normally have one minute to make notes and then speak for one to two minutes. The examiner may ask a brief question after your talk before moving to Part 3.

rows: What it means for your talk
Focus on the central topic rather than trying to cover every possible angle.
Use them as a checklist for relevant content, not as four separate mini-answers.
Write keywords, names, times, places and useful phrases—not complete sentences.
Develop a connected talk with a beginning, middle and ending.
Develop the topic sufficiently; do not add irrelevant details just to fill time.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE • Cue card: Describe a useful skill you learned. You should say what it is, when and how you learned it, who helped you, and explain why it is useful. Notes: basic cooking / last summer / watched family member, practised weekends / independence, saves money.
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES • The cue card supplies the topic and directions. Select connected details and develop them into a coherent talk.
2. Read the cue card strategically
Identify the main topic noun phrase, notice the instruction verb (describe, talk about, explain), then scan the bullet points and decide what information each one asks for.

rows: Who they are, how you know them, qualities, a specific example, why they matter.
Listing adjectives without showing them through an example.
Location, appearance, atmosphere, what you do there, why it matters.
Giving only an address or general opinion.
When and where, people involved, sequence, outcome, feelings and significance.
Jumping between events without a clear timeline.
What it is, how you got it, appearance/use, personal value.
Describing appearance but ignoring its importance.
What it involves, how you started, frequency, benefits or challenges.
Explaining the activity generally but not your own experience.
Situation, options, choice, reasons, result and reflection.
Saying only what you chose without explaining why.

theory.text: 3. Use a flexible structure: Opening → Development → Reflection
This is a planning aid, not a rigid formula. Adapt it to the topic.

rows: Name the topic and establish context.
I’d like to talk about… / The first thing that comes to mind is…
Add details, an example, a sequence or a contrast.
What I remember most is… / At first… but later…
Explain why it mattered, how you felt or what changed.
Looking back… / What made it memorable was… / Since then…

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE • “I’d like to talk about a day trip I took with two friends last year. We left early, visited a coastal town and tried a local dish. The weather changed in the afternoon, so we spent some time in a small café. It was memorable because we had time to talk without worrying about university deadlines.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES • The talk has a clear starting point, connected details and a reflection. It does not need a dramatic story to be interesting.
4. Make useful notes in one minute
Use notes as memory triggers. Divide the page into context, main details, example or sequence, and meaning or feelings.

rows: Minh / classmate / helped coding project / stayed after class / patient
Specific cues trigger a concrete example.
last summer → first attempt → difficult → practised weekly → improved
Keywords are quicker to write and easier to speak from.
A focused talk is easier to follow.

theory.text: Write nouns, verbs, dates and adjectives—not every connecting word.
Choose details you can explain comfortably; an ordinary experience is fine.
Make sure the notes cover the cue-card prompts.
Leave a few seconds to check the order and final point.
5. Develop ideas instead of listing them
Turn each keyword into a small unit: make a point, explain it, and add an example or consequence. For stories, use sequence; for people and places, group related details.

rows: “She is patient. When I struggled with a presentation, she helped me practise twice.”
Makes an event easy to follow.
At first… / A little later… / By the end…
Explains why something happened or mattered.
Because I practised regularly, I became more confident.
I used to avoid speaking, but now I volunteer more often.
The experience taught me to ask for help earlier.

theory.text: 6. Keep the talk coherent

rows: I’d like to talk about… / The example I have in mind is…
Another thing I remember is… / What stands out is…
Do not repeat the same point.
Use when there is a real timeline.
The main reason was… / This was partly because…
Looking back… / That’s why… / Since then…
Avoid a conclusion that repeats everything.

theory.text: 7. Use topic vocabulary naturally
A few precise collocations are usually more helpful than several rare words. Choose language you can pronounce and use accurately.

rows: reliable, easy to get along with, give practical advice, set a good example
“He gives practical advice without making me feel embarrassed.”
peaceful atmosphere, within walking distance, get away from the crowds
“It has a peaceful atmosphere, especially early in the morning.”
step out of my comfort zone, a sense of achievement, things did not go to plan
“Finishing the project gave me a sense of achievement.”
come in handy, sentimental value, rely on, practical purpose
“It comes in handy when I need to take notes.”
pick up a skill, make steady progress, learn through trial and error
“I learned through trial and error rather than a formal course.”
look forward to, get together, go smoothly, a change of pace
“The celebration was a welcome change of pace after exams.”

theory.text: 8. Grammar choices for a long turn

rows: “We were walking back when it started to rain.”
“I used to be nervous about speaking in public.”
“I’d like to visit again if I get the chance.”
Relative clauses: who / which / that / where
“It’s a café where I often study.”

theory.text: Do not force every tense into one answer. Choose grammar that matches the time and meaning.
9. Fluency, pronunciation and recovery
Speak at a manageable pace; fluency is not speaking as fast as possible.
Group words into meaningful chunks rather than pausing after every word.
If you forget a detail, move on to another relevant point instead of restarting.
If you do not know a word, explain it in simpler language.
Record yourself and listen for long silences, repeated ideas and unclear word endings.
WORKED EXAMPLE • If you forget a place name: “I can’t remember the name of the café, but it was a small place near the river, and it had a lovely view.”
10. Common mistakes to avoid

rows: Uses the minute for writing rather than planning.
Write keywords and a clear sequence.
The talk sounds like a list.
Use an opening and connect details.
Hard to remember and deliver naturally.
Use a plausible experience and develop it.
Give an example, result or reflection.
Explain one detail or why it mattered.
Aim for a sufficiently developed talk.

theory.text: 11. Assessment criteria in practical terms

rows: Maintain a natural pace, organise the talk and link ideas clearly.
Use relevant vocabulary and collocations; paraphrase when a word is missing.
Use accurate sentences and a suitable range of structures and tenses.
Make words intelligible; use clear stress, chunking and a manageable pace.

theory.text: These are study explanations, not a band-score calculator. A single practice talk cannot reliably determine an overall Speaking band.
12. A 10-second checklist
Have I identified the central topic?
Do my notes cover the cue-card prompts?
Is there a clear order?
Do I have specific details or an example?
Can I explain why it matters or how I felt?
Are my notes keywords rather than a script?

guide.text: Part 3 – Planning guide
The aim is to prepare a route for your talk, not to write a memorised speech. Give yourself one minute and write keywords only. Then look away from the notes and speak.
A reusable one-minute planning worksheet

rows: When? Where? Who was involved? How did it begin?
What are two details or actions worth describing?
What specific moment, challenge or example can I explain?
Why does it matter? How did I feel? What changed?
Do the notes cover the prompts and follow a clear order?

guide.text: Worked planning example
Cue card: Describe a skill you would like to learn.
Possible opening • “A skill I’d really like to develop is photography, particularly taking better pictures when I travel.”
How to use the plan • The notes suggest motivation, a learning method, a challenge and personal value. They are not complete sentences.
Planning worksheets P1–P10
P1. A person who influenced you
Plan with keywords: Who they are / how you know them / specific thing they did / influence.
P2. A place you enjoy visiting
Plan with keywords: Location / atmosphere / what you do / memorable detail / why you return.
P3. A useful object
Plan with keywords: What it is / how you got it / how you use it / example / why it matters.
P4. A memorable day
Plan with keywords: When and where / people / sequence / best moment / feelings.
P5. A skill you learned
Plan with keywords: Skill / when and why / how you learned / challenge / result.
P6. A time you helped someone
Plan with keywords: Who / situation / what you did / response / feelings.
P7. A celebration
Plan with keywords: What was celebrated / where and with whom / activities / atmosphere / significance.
P8. A film or book
Plan with keywords: Title/type / when experienced / main idea / favourite part / recommendation.
P9. A journey
Plan with keywords: Destination / reason / travel method / event or view / impression.
P10. A goal you achieved
Plan with keywords: Goal / reason / steps / obstacle / result and lesson.
How to review a plan
Can I identify the topic in the first sentence?
Do the notes cover each cue-card prompt?
Is there a logical sequence or grouping?
Do I have a specific example, not just adjectives?
Does the final point explain significance, feelings or a lesson?
Can I speak without reading complete sentences?

small.text: Part 2 – Small exercises
Complete these tasks before checking the suggested answers. Say responses aloud when the task involves speaking. Times are practice estimates.
E1. Identify the cue-card focus
Allow 5 minutes. Identify the main topic and the information the talk should cover.
Describe a person who has influenced you. Say who the person is, how you know them, what they have done, and how they influenced you.
Describe a useful object you own. Say what it is, how you got it, how you use it, and why it is useful.
Describe a time you tried something new. Say what you tried, when and where you did it, who was with you, and how you felt.
Describe a place you like to visit. Say where it is, what it is like, what you do there, and why you like it.
E2. Turn vague notes into useful notes
Allow 6 minutes. Improve each weak note set by adding an action, place, time, person or result.
E3. Put a story in order
Allow 4 minutes. Arrange the notes into a logical order, then tell the story in 5–7 sentences.

A. finally finished the presentation and felt relieved • B. realised the slides were incomplete the night before • C. practised the opening with a classmate • D. gave a university presentation last semester • E. divided the remaining work and corrected the slides
E4. Develop a keyword
Allow 8 minutes. Choose three topics. Speak two or three sentences for each: point → explanation → example or result.
patient teacher
crowded market
old photograph
learning to cycle
team project
E5. Add reflection
Allow 6 minutes. Add a sentence explaining why each experience mattered. Avoid simply repeating “It was good.”
I learned to cook a simple meal on my own. → Reflection: __________________________________________
A friend helped me prepare for an exam. → Reflection: __________________________________________
I visited a quiet place after a stressful week. → Reflection: __________________________________________
I completed a difficult assignment. → Reflection: __________________________________________
E6. Choose a useful structure

rows: A. Description → use → why it matters
D. Starting point → practice/challenge → progress → benefit

small.text: E7. Replace repetition with detail
Allow 6 minutes. Rewrite each weak line so it adds new information.
“The place was nice. It was really nice, and I liked it because it was nice.”
“My cousin is helpful. He is very helpful and always helps me.”
“The trip was exciting. It was exciting from beginning to end.”
E8. Paraphrase when a word is missing
Allow 6 minutes. Explain the idea without using the key word. Aim for one or two natural sentences.
“I borrowed a tripod to keep my camera steady.”
“We went to a waterfall during our holiday.”
“She gave me a handwritten note before I left.”
“I felt overwhelmed when I had several deadlines.”
E9. One-minute planning drill
Allow 8 minutes. Take exactly one minute to plan. Use keywords only, then speak for 60–90 seconds.
Describe a time you helped someone. Say who you helped, what the situation was, what you did, and how you felt about helping them.
E10. Diagnose the problem
Identify the main weakness: no clear structure, too vague, repetitive, tense mismatch, overcomplicated language, or insufficient reflection. Suggest one improvement.
“I want to talk about a person. He is good. He is very good. I like him.”
“Last year I go to a competition and I was nervous.”
“First, there was a thing, and then something happened, and it was amazing.”
“This extraordinary individual constitutes an indispensable component of my personal development.”
A talk describes what a gift looks like but never says who gave it or why it matters.

review.text: Part 5 – Complete answer key

These are suggestions, not the only correct responses. Personalise the details and use your own truthful experiences. The model talks demonstrate organisation and development, not official examiner responses.
Answers for E1
Person/influence: identify the person, relationship, action or quality, and its effect on you.
Useful object: identify it, how you obtained it, its practical use, and why it helps.
New experience: name the activity, establish when/where and who was there, describe what happened, and explain your feelings.
Place: identify the location, describe its atmosphere, explain what you do there, and give a personal reason.
Suggested approaches for E2–E8

rows: Friend: classmate / explained a difficult topic / before exam / helped me prepare. Park: near home / shaded path / walk after class / quiet in evening. Phone: bought last year / timetable and messages / daily use / keeps tasks organised. Trip: coastal town / last summer / bus with friends / unexpected rain / café stop.
D → B → E → C → A. Start with context, introduce the problem, explain the response, mention preparation and finish with the outcome.

Patient teacher: explain a difficult idea with an example. Crowded market: describe sounds and what you bought. Old photograph: say who is in it and what memory it brings back. Learning to cycle: describe first attempt, difficulty and progress. Team project: explain your role and result.
Example: “It mattered because I realised I could manage a basic task independently.” Explain a lesson, change, relationship or personal meaning.
Memorable event → B. Person you admire → C. Useful object → A. Skill learned → D.

Place: “It had a quiet garden and a view of the river, so I stayed there to read.” Cousin: “He checked my slides and practised questions with me.” Trip: “We missed the bus, found another route and arrived just before sunset.”

Tripod: a three-legged stand that holds a camera still. Waterfall: a place where water flows over a high edge of rock. Handwritten: written by hand rather than typed. Overwhelmed: feeling as if everything is too much to deal with at once.

rows: Name the person and give an action that shows why you like them.
“Last year I went to a competition and felt nervous.”
No clear structure and vague detail
Describe a specific event in chronological order.
Use natural words and a concrete example.
Explain how you got the gift and why it is meaningful, not only its appearance.

P1 Person: older cousin / helped choose study path / honest and patient / reviewed first project / more confident
P2 Place: small park near home / trees and lake / walk after class / quiet at sunset / clear my head
P3 Object: laptop / family gift before university / coding and assignments / daily use / supports learning
P4 Memorable day: last birthday / dinner with family / surprise visit from friend / photos and cake / felt appreciated
P5 Skill: basic cooking / wanted independence / tutorials and practice / first meals too salty / now useful
P6 Help: classmate / missed lesson / shared notes / studied together / friendship strengthened
P7 Celebration: family wedding / restaurant / relatives travelled / speeches and music / brought family together
P8 Film/book: film about friendship / watched during holiday / difficult choice / emotional ending / made me reflect
P9 Journey: weekend trip to coast / bus / scenery and local food / chatted with friends / relaxing break
P10 Goal: finish course project / career relevance / weekly milestones / debugging / proud and organised
Model talks for full practice sets
F1. A person who influenced you

I’d like to talk about my older cousin, who has influenced the way I approach studying. I’ve known him all my life, but I started asking him for advice more often when I entered university. He is patient and practical, and he doesn’t simply tell me what to do. Instead, he asks questions that help me work things out. I remember struggling with a programming assignment and feeling that I wasn’t making progress. He suggested breaking the task into smaller parts and testing each part separately. That made it easier to manage. I admire him because he stays calm when something goes wrong, and I’ve tried to develop the same habit. His influence matters because it has changed how I study and how I deal with difficult situations.
F2. A place you like to visit

A place I enjoy visiting is a small park not far from where I live. It isn’t a famous tourist attraction, but it has trees, walking paths and a quiet area where people can sit. I usually go there in the late afternoon, especially after studying indoors for several hours. Sometimes I walk around while listening to music; on other days I sit on a bench and read. What I like most is the atmosphere. Even though the surrounding area can be busy, the park feels calmer, particularly near sunset. It gives me a chance to clear my head and take a break from screens. I keep returning because I don’t need to plan anything, and even a short visit makes the rest of my day feel more manageable.
F3. A useful object

One object I find very useful is my laptop. I got it before starting university because I needed a reliable device for programming, assignments and online learning. I use it almost every day, whether I’m writing code, reading course materials or attending an online meeting. The most useful thing is that it keeps many parts of my study routine in one place. For example, when I work on a project, I can edit code, look up documentation and write notes without switching devices. It can be distracting if I open too many websites, so I close unnecessary tabs when I need to concentrate. Overall, it is more than an electronic device; it is an important tool that supports my studies and helps me practise skills outside class.
F4. A memorable day

A memorable day was a birthday I celebrated with my family last year. We didn’t organise a big party; instead, we had dinner at a restaurant we all liked and spent the evening talking. What made the day special was that a close friend turned up unexpectedly after dinner. I hadn’t seen them for a while because we were both busy with our studies. We took photos, shared a cake and talked about what had been happening in our lives. The event was simple, but I felt appreciated because people close to me had made time to be there. I remember it when I’m stressed because it reminds me that meaningful moments don’t have to be expensive or carefully planned.
F5. A skill you learned

A practical skill I learned is cooking a few simple meals. I started learning when my schedule became busier and I realised that buying every meal could be expensive. At first, I watched short online tutorials and tried easy dishes such as fried rice and noodles. My first attempts weren’t very successful; sometimes the food was too salty or I cooked it for too long. However, I kept practising at weekends and gradually learned to prepare ingredients in advance and control the heat. I still wouldn’t call myself an excellent cook, but I can make something decent without following every instruction. The skill gives me independence and helps me save money. It has also taught me that improvement often comes from making small mistakes and learning from them.
F6. A time you helped someone

I remember helping a classmate who missed a lesson shortly before a test. They were worried because the topic was difficult, so I shared my notes and offered to explain the main ideas after class. We sat in the library and went through examples one by one. When my classmate didn’t understand something, I tried explaining it differently rather than repeating the same words. It took longer than I expected, but by the end they seemed more confident and could solve a few practice questions independently. I felt glad that I could help, partly because I knew how stressful it was to fall behind. The experience also helped me because explaining the material showed me which parts I understood and which parts I needed to review.
F7. A celebration

One celebration I enjoyed was a family wedding a couple of years ago. It took place at a restaurant, and relatives travelled from different places to attend. Before the meal, we greeted one another and took photos. Later, there were speeches, music and plenty of food. I particularly enjoyed seeing relatives I hadn’t met for a long time, because everyone had stories to share. The celebration was lively, but what mattered most was the feeling of being together. People in my family are normally busy with work or study, so it can be difficult to find a day when everyone is available. I remember the wedding because it gave the family a reason to reconnect.
F8. A film or book

A film I remember well is one about friendship and making difficult choices. I watched it at home during a holiday after a friend recommended it. I don’t remember every detail of the plot, but the main character had to choose between an easy option and doing what they believed was right. What stood out was how the decision affected their relationships. The acting was convincing, and the story moved at a steady pace, so I stayed interested until the end. I liked it because it was entertaining but also gave me something to think about afterwards. It reminded me that doing the right thing is not always comfortable, especially when other people disagree. I’d recommend it to someone who enjoys character-driven stories.
F9. A journey

A journey I enjoyed was a weekend trip to a coastal town with two friends. We travelled by bus because it was affordable and none of us had to worry about driving. The journey took a few hours, but I didn’t find it boring because we chatted, listened to music and watched the scenery change. After arriving, we walked near the beach, tried local food and took photos before the weather became too hot. My favourite part was having time away from our usual routines. We were all busy with university, so the trip felt like a proper break. I enjoyed it because the plan was simple and flexible; we didn’t have to rush between attractions and could spend longer wherever we liked.
F10. A goal you achieved

One goal I achieved was completing a challenging university project on time. I wanted to do well because it involved concepts I hoped to use in future work, but at first it seemed difficult alongside my other subjects. I divided the work into smaller tasks, set deadlines for each stage and tested my work regularly instead of leaving everything until the end. The biggest challenge was debugging a problem that kept returning, so I checked documentation and tested several solutions. When the project finally worked, I felt relieved and proud. More importantly, I learned that planning is only useful if I check progress and adjust when something takes longer than expected. That lesson has helped me approach later assignments more calmly.
F11. A time you tried something new

A time I tried something new was when I joined a beginner photography walk with a friend. I usually take pictures casually on my phone, so I wanted to learn how to frame a shot more carefully. We met at a park on a weekend morning and took photos of trees, buildings and people from different angles. At first, I paid too much attention to the subject and forgot to check the background, so several pictures looked messy. My friend showed me how moving a step to one side could make a big difference. I enjoyed the experience because it was relaxed and practical. It reminded me that trying a new activity doesn’t have to involve a major commitment; a small experiment can be enough to discover an interest.
F12. Someone you would like to work or study with

I’d like to work or study with a lecturer I’ve seen explaining technical topics online. I don’t know them personally, but I appreciate the way they break complicated ideas into manageable steps and use practical examples. They show not only the correct solution but also mistakes beginners tend to make. I think that approach would be useful in a group project because people can understand the reasoning rather than just copy a result. I’d like to ask how they choose which problems are worth exploring and how they keep learning in a fast-changing field. I’d like to work with them because I value people who are knowledgeable but also willing to explain things clearly. I think I could learn technical skills and better ways of communicating.
Self-assessment checklist
☐ I introduced the topic clearly.
☐ I covered the cue-card prompts.
☐ I organised details logically.
☐ I gave at least one specific example or moment.
☐ I explained why the topic mattered or how I felt.
☐ I used relevant vocabulary naturally.
☐ My grammar and tenses matched the meaning.
☐ I spoke clearly and avoided unnecessary pauses.
☐ I used notes as prompts rather than reading a script.
